title: Practice Passage 6: The Role of Epigenetics in Genetics

passage.title: The Role of Epigenetics in Genetics
passage.sub_title: Understanding how environmental factors can alter gene expression without changing the primary DNA sequence.
passage.content_html:
For decades, the dominant paradigm in biology was that our genes determine our physical traits and health outcomes. According to this deterministic view, the DNA sequence we inherit from our parents is a fixed blueprint, and our biological destiny is largely pre-determined. However, the emerging field of epigenetics has challenged this traditional view. Epigenetics, which literally translates to 'above genetics', is the study of cellular and physiological trait variations that are not caused by changes in the underlying DNA sequence. Instead, it focuses on how environmental factors, such as diet, stress, and toxins, can modify gene expression, turning genes on or off like light switches.

To understand epigenetics, it is helpful to look at the structure of DNA inside the cell. If stretched out, the DNA in a single human cell would be about two metres long. To fit inside the microscopic nucleus, DNA is tightly wound around packaging proteins called histones. This DNA-protein complex is known as chromatin. Chemical tags attached to either the DNA itself or to the histones determine how tightly the DNA is wound. When DNA is wrapped tightly around histones, the molecular machinery of the cell cannot access it, meaning the gene is effectively silenced. Conversely, when the chromatin structure is relaxed, the genes are exposed and can be read by the cell to produce proteins.

The two most thoroughly studied epigenetic mechanisms are DNA methylation and histone modification. DNA methylation involves the attachment of small chemical tags, called methyl groups, directly to the DNA molecule, usually silencing the gene. Histone modification, on the other hand, involves the addition of chemical tags (such as acetyl groups) to histones, which can either tighten or loosen the chromatin structure. These chemical tags are collectively referred to as the 'epigenome'. While the genome remains identical across all cells in an individual's body, the epigenome varies widely between different cell types, allowing a skin cell to function differently from a brain cell despite carrying the exact same DNA.

Epigenetic changes are not only vital for normal development, but they also play a significant role in disease. For example, in many cancers, the normal pattern of DNA methylation is disrupted. Genes that would normally prevent cancer cells from growing (tumor suppressor genes) are often hypermethylated, meaning they are permanently turned off. Conversely, genes that promote cell growth (oncogenes) may be hypomethylated, causing them to become overactive. Researchers are now developing epigenetic therapies that aim to remove these abnormal chemical tags, effectively turning cancer-fighting genes back on.

Perhaps the most controversial aspect of epigenetics is the discovery that some epigenetic marks can be inherited across generations. Historically, it was believed that when an egg and sperm fuse, all epigenetic tags are erased, resetting the embryo to a clean slate. However, studies on plants, rodents, and even humans suggest that some epigenetic modifications survive this resetting process. A famous study of the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–1945 showed that children conceived during the famine had unique epigenetic tags that altered their metabolism, making them more prone to obesity and cardiovascular disease in adulthood. Surprisingly, some of these traits were also observed in their children, suggesting that the starvation of grandparents can leave a biological mark on grandchildren.
